theme: David’s victories; the ark in Jerusalem; the covenant
readingInstruction: Read 1 Chronicles 14:1-17:27. The ark comes to Jerusalem with joy, David sings a great psalm of thanksgiving, and God makes his covenant with David. Read chapter 16 as worship and chapter 17 as promise.
settingTheScene: After the failure of the first attempt, David prepares a tent for the ark and has the Levites carry it properly. The procession is a feast of music and dancing. David then appoints Asaph and his brothers to give thanks daily before the ark. Then David, living in a house of cedar, wants to build a house for God, and God responds with a covenant that is the pivot of the whole Bible: God will build David a house.
observation: “For none but the Levites may carry the ark of God” (15:2).
“Thus all Israel brought up the ark of the covenant of the LORD with shouting, to the sound of the horn, trumpets, and cymbals, and made loud music on harps and lyres” (15:28).
“On that day David first appointed that thanksgiving be sung to the LORD by Asaph and his brothers” (16:7).
“Oh give thanks to the LORD; call upon his name; make known his deeds among the peoples!” (16:8).
“Sing to the LORD, all the earth! Tell of his salvation from day to day” (16:23).
“Moreover, I declare to you that the LORD will build you a house” (17:10).
“I will raise up your offspring after you… and I will establish his kingdom” (17:11).
interpretation:
This time David does it right. The Levites carry the ark on their shoulders, as the law prescribed. The music and sacrifices are offered. David even dances in joy, which his wife Michal despises, though the Chronicler does not dwell on it. The ark is placed in the tent David prepared, and then David delivers a psalm that is a compilation of what we know as parts of Psalms 105, 96, and 106. It is a missionary hymn: “Make known his deeds among the peoples! Sing to the LORD, all the earth! Declare his glory among the nations.” David was not satisfied with a local, tribal religion. His praise reached to all peoples.

The psalm ends with the refrain that you memorized at the weekly rest: “Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever.” Then comes the daily ministry of the Levites. The worship of Israel was constant.

Then comes chapter 17, the greatest moment. David says, “I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of the covenant of the LORD is under a tent.” He wants to build a house for God. God, through Nathan, turns it around: you will not build a house for me, but I will build a house for you. A dynasty. “I will raise up your offspring after you, one of your own sons, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for me, and I will establish his throne forever.” Solomon will build the temple, but the promise reaches farther. The Chronicler, writing after the monarchy ended, holds on to this promise. The throne of David will be established forever, and that can only be fulfilled in someone greater than any of David’s sons. 

David’s response is a model prayer: “Who am I, O LORD God, and what is my house, that you have brought me thus far?” It is humility before grace.
connection: Luke 1:32-33: the angel says that the Lord God will give Jesus the throne of his father David, and “of his kingdom there will be no end.” Hebrews 1:5 quotes “I will be to him a father” from this chapter. Acts 13:22-23 connects David and Jesus. Matthew 28:19 sends the church to all nations. Romans 15:9-11 shows the nations praising God. Psalm 89:3-4 recalls the covenant with David.
application:
Make the praise of 16:8-36 your own. Read it aloud and mention God’s deeds in your life.

Ask: who might I tell about God’s deeds this week? Make known his deeds among the peoples.

Pray David’s prayer: “Who am I, O LORD God, that you have brought me thus far?”
prayerPrompts: Give thanks to God and call upon his name.
Ask him to help you make known his deeds among the nations.
Thank him for the covenant he made with David.
